title: Je m'appelle…
goal: Say your name, ask someone's name in a friendly or formal way, and react when you meet someone.

items.en: to be called (present: je, tu, il/elle, vous)

blocks.title: A French class for newcomers in Gatineau
blocks.context: Lucie, the teacher, meets her new students. Later, two students chat at the break.

lines.speaker: Lucie
lines.fr: Et vous, monsieur ? Comment vous appelez-vous ?
lines.en: And you, sir? What's your name?

lines.speaker: Lucie
lines.en: Mei… How do you spell it?

lines.speaker: Lucie
lines.fr: Merci. Ravie de vous rencontrer, Mei.
lines.en: Thank you. Pleased to meet you, Mei.

lines.speaker: Mei
lines.fr: Salut, Karim ! Et elle, elle s'appelle comment ?
lines.en: Hi, Karim! And what about her? What's her name?

blocks.body: Listen first. Notice that Lucie says [[vous]] to her students, but Karim and Mei say [[salut]] and talk like friends.

blocks.title: S'appeler: “to be called”
blocks.body:
The usual French way to give your name is not “my name is” but **“I call myself”**: [[je m'appelle]].

The verb is [[s'appeler]]. The little word in front ([[m']], [[t']], [[s']], [[vous]]) changes with the person, like *myself*, *yourself*, *herself*. You'll meet more verbs like this later; for now, learn these forms as chunks.

blocks.title: S'appeler in the present
head: s'appeler
English
rows: your name is (formal, or more than one person)
blocks.note: [[m'appelle]], [[t'appelles]] and [[s'appelle]] sound the same: *a-PEL*. Only [[vous vous appelez]] sounds different: *vou-za-PLÉ*.

blocks.title: Asking someone's name
blocks.pattern: formal: Comment vous appelez-vous ? · friendly: Comment tu t'appelles ?
blocks.note: Both questions have a **spoken** version with [[comment]] at the end. It is very common in real conversation.

examples.en: What's your name? (formal, a bit careful)
What's your name? (to a friend or a child)

blocks.title: When you meet someone
blocks.pattern: Enchanté(e) ! · Ravi(e) de vous rencontrer. · Moi, c'est…
blocks.note: Women add **-e** in writing: [[enchantée]], [[ravie]]. You can't hear the difference.

examples.en: Nice to meet you! I'm Raj.
Nice to meet you, Olivier. (woman speaking)
Pleased to meet you, ma'am. (woman speaking)

blocks.body:
Why two l's in [[appelle]] but one in [[appelez]]?

- With **two l's**, the e before them sounds like *è*: [[je m'appelle]] = *je ma-PEL*.
- With **one l**, that e almost disappears: [[vous vous appelez]] = *vou vou-za-PLÉ*.

The spelling is showing you the sound. Also notice the liaison: [[vous‿appelez]] has a *z* sound.

examples.en: my name is — your name is (formal)

blocks.body:
- **Forgetting the little word:** [[J'appelle Karim]] means “I'm calling Karim” (on the phone)! Say [[Je m'appelle Karim]].
- **Mixing two structures:** [[Je m'appelle est Mei]] is wrong. Say [[Je m'appelle Mei]] or [[Moi, c'est Mei]].
- **Tu and vous together:** [[Comment tu vous appelez ?]] mixes two people. Choose one: [[Comment tu t'appelles ?]] or [[Comment vous appelez-vous ?]]
- **One l / two l's:** write [[je m'appelle]] but [[vous vous appelez]].

In Québec, people often switch to [[tu]] quickly, even with new colleagues, and [[Moi, c'est…]] is a very common way to give your name. With an official, a doctor or an older person, start with [[vous]] and let them suggest [[tu]].

You'll also hear [[Mon nom, c'est…]] in Québec. It's understood everywhere, but [[je m'appelle]] is the safest choice.

On Canadian forms, [[Nom]] means your **last name** and [[Prénom]] your **first name**. Don't write your first name in the [[Nom]] box!

examples.en: Last name: Tremblay. First name: Lucie.

blocks.title: With a friend: te instead of vous
blocks.body: [[Ravi de vous rencontrer]] is formal. With someone you call [[tu]], the [[vous]] becomes [[te]]: [[Ravi de te rencontrer]]. Many people simply say [[Enchanté !]] in both situations.

examples.en: Nice to meet you, Alex! (woman speaking, to a friend)

blocks.title: Listen and repeat
blocks.note: Say each line out loud. Then record yourself and compare.

lines.tip: Link the words: vou-z‿appelez; appelez sounds like “a-PLAY”.

blocks.prompt: It's your first French class. Introduce yourself to the teacher (use vous), then turn to the student next to you and ask their name (use tu).
checklist: Ask the teacher: Comment vous appelez-vous ?
Ask the student: Tu t'appelles comment ?

models.label: Model answer
models.fr: Bonjour, madame ! Je m'appelle Raj. Comment vous appelez-vous ? … Enchanté ! … Salut ! Moi, c'est Raj. Tu t'appelles comment ? … Enchanté, Mei !
models.en: Hello, ma'am! My name is Raj. What's your name? … Nice to meet you! … Hi! I'm Raj. What's your name? … Nice to meet you, Mei!

blocks.prompt: Write a short first message in your class group chat: say hello, give your name, spell it, and ask a classmate's name.
checklist: A question with tu: Tu t'appelles comment ?

models.label: Model answer
models.fr: Salut à tous ! Je m'appelle Nguyen : N-G-U-Y-E-N. Et toi ? Tu t'appelles comment ?
models.en: Hi everyone! My name is Nguyen: N-G-U-Y-E-N. And you? What's your name?

models.label: Shorter model
models.fr: Bonjour ! Moi, c'est Amira. Enchantée ! Et toi, tu t'appelles comment ?
models.en: Hello! I'm Amira. Nice to meet you! And you, what's your name?

summary:
- Say your name with [[je m'appelle…]] or [[moi, c'est…]]
- Ask a name politely ([[Comment vous appelez-vous ?]]) or in a friendly way ([[Tu t'appelles comment ?]])
- Say who someone is: [[il s'appelle…]], [[elle s'appelle…]]
- React with [[Enchanté(e) !]] and [[Ravi(e) de vous rencontrer]]
